client: I've been really struggling with anxiety about my final exams coming up. After getting a C on my last psychology paper, I can't stop worrying that I'm going to fail everything. I know therapy is supposed to help with anxiety, but I'm not sure talking about it will change the fact that my grades might tank.
therapist: I hear how worried you are about your exams, especially after that psychology paper didn't go as well as you'd hoped. It makes sense you'd feel anxious when so much feels at stake right now. What thoughts go through your mind when you picture yourself taking these exams?

client: I just keep imagining myself blanking out during the exams and failing everything. My mind keeps replaying that moment when I got my last paper back and saw the C - I feel like that's proof I'm not smart enough for this program. I know I should study more but I can't even focus because of these thoughts.
therapist: It sounds like that C grade has become strong evidence for your mind that you're not capable, even though I know from our sessions how much effort and intelligence you actually have. When those thoughts about not being smart enough come up, how do they typically affect your ability to focus on studying?

client: When those thoughts hit, I just freeze up. I'll open my textbook but then start thinking "what's the point if I'm going to fail anyway" and end up scrolling on my phone for hours. Part of me knows that's irrational, but it feels impossible to push through when I'm convinced I'm not good enough.
therapist: It sounds like those thoughts create a cycle where the more you doubt yourself, the harder it becomes to study, which then reinforces those doubts. What would it feel like to try a small experiment where you set a timer for just 15 minutes of focused study, noticing those thoughts but letting them pass without judgment?

client: I don't know if I could even focus for 15 minutes with these thoughts swirling around. Every time I try to study, it's like my mind keeps pulling me back to worrying about failing. Maybe I could try it, but I'm not sure it would actually help break this cycle.
therapist: It's understandable that focusing feels so difficult when your mind keeps pulling you back into worry. These thoughts feel very convincing right now, but they don't have to control your actions. What would it be like to notice those thoughts without fighting them, almost like watching clouds pass by, while you gently bring your attention back to your study materials?

client: I guess I could try seeing my thoughts as just passing clouds, but it feels like these particular clouds have roots digging into my brain, you know? When I think "I'm going to fail," it doesn't feel like a passing thought - it feels like a fact. Still... maybe noticing how intense my reaction is could be a first step?
therapist: I really appreciate your willingness to explore this approach, even while acknowledging how deeply rooted these thoughts feel right now. You're right - noticing the intensity of your reaction is a meaningful first step in creating some space between you and those thoughts. What do you notice happens physically in your body when those "I'm going to fail" thoughts feel most intense and factual?

client: My chest gets really tight, and my hands start shaking. Sometimes I even feel nauseous, like before an exam. It's hard to imagine being able to study when my body reacts this strongly - makes me just want to crawl into bed and avoid everything.
therapist: Those physical reactions sound really intense and understandably make studying feel impossible in those moments. It might help to notice that your body is reacting as if there's immediate danger, even though you're actually safe at your desk. What would it feel like to try some slow, deep breathing when those physical symptoms start, just to see what happens?

client: I've tried breathing exercises before when I get like this, but then I just start thinking "I'm wasting time breathing when I should be studying" and it makes me more anxious. It's like my brain finds new ways to panic no matter what I try.
therapist: It sounds like your mind is very good at finding reasons why any coping strategy won't work, which must feel exhausting. What if we viewed that critical thought as just another passing cloud, noticing it without arguing with it or believing it completely?

client: You know, when you put it that way, it's like my anxiety keeps moving the goalposts. Even when I try to help myself, my brain finds a way to turn that into more stress. It's frustrating because part of me wants these techniques to work, but another part keeps sabotaging them.
therapist: You're noticing such an important pattern here - how your anxiety finds ways to undermine even your attempts to feel better. That inner conflict between wanting help and self-sabotage must feel so frustrating. What would it be like to simply observe this pattern with curiosity rather than judgment for the next few days?

client: Observing with curiosity sounds better than beating myself up, but it feels hard to stay neutral when my grades are on the line. I'm worried that if I just observe without trying to fix things, I'll fall even further behind with my studying.
therapist: It's completely understandable to feel that urgency when your grades are so important to you. That pressure makes it hard to just observe without wanting to fix things immediately. What would it feel like to try a small experiment where you spend just 5 minutes observing your thoughts and feelings before diving into studying, noticing if it changes anything about how you approach your work?

client: I could try 5 minutes, but I'm skeptical it'll make any difference. It feels like another thing to add to my already overwhelming study routine. What if I just end up more anxious after noticing all my worries instead of ignoring them?
therapist: You're absolutely right to point out that adding anything new right now feels overwhelming, and I appreciate your honesty about the skepticism. Maybe instead of viewing this as another task, we could think of it as hitting the pause button before studying—what do you imagine might be different if you approached it that way?
